parts.text:
1
How many cubic nanometres, nm3, are in a cubic micrometre, µm3?
A
103
B
106
C
109
D
1012

hints: Recall what the prefixes mean in metres: $1 \, \mu\text{m} = 10^{-6} \, \text{m}$ and $1 \, \text{nm} = 10^{-9} \, \text{m}$, so find how many nanometres fit along one micrometre edge.
Convert the length first: divide $10^{-6} \, \text{m}$ by $10^{-9} \, \text{m}$ to get the number of $\text{nm}$ in $1 \, \mu\text{m}$.
The question asks for $\mu\text{m}^3$ to $\text{nm}^3$, a volume, so cube the length ratio you found rather than using it directly.
walkthrough: Write each prefix in metres: $1 \, \mu\text{m} = 10^{-6} \, \text{m}$ and $1 \, \text{nm} = 10^{-9} \, \text{m}$.
Find the linear conversion by dividing: $\dfrac{10^{-6} \, \text{m}}{10^{-9} \, \text{m}} = 10^3$, so $1 \, \mu\text{m} = 10^3 \, \text{nm}$.
For a cube, volume = (side length)$^3$, so $1 \, \mu\text{m}^3 = (10^3 \, \text{nm})^3$.

A.explanation: This is only the linear ratio $1 \, \mu\text{m} = 10^3 \, \text{nm}$. Volume needs this factor cubed.

B.explanation: This squares the linear factor $10^3$, giving an area conversion. A cubic volume needs the cube of $10^3$.

D.explanation: This is too large by $10^3$ and comes from cubing $10^4$ instead of the correct linear factor $10^3$.
